Code × Motion × Interfaces

One source.
An interface in motion.

Anima is a small, browser-based language for composing interface structure, styling, motion, sound, and scene navigation in one readable source file. This guide documents the parser and runtime that ship with the current project—not just the vision.

Custom DSLBrowser runtimeNo build stepOffline-friendly
01 /Describe structure

Build nested nodes inside scenes using concise, named properties.

02 /Compose motion

Attach named entrances and combine animations with a small operator set.

03 /Connect actions

React to pointer and focus events, navigate between scenes, and play generated chimes.

01 / Quick start

Get a page on screen.

The simplest route is to save the runtime JavaScript, create a mount element, write an Anima program as a string, then call Anima.parse() and Anima.mount(). No bundler or package manager is required.

✳
Start from this folder. The downloadable documentation bundle includes the exact runtime extracted from the current Anima HTML project, plus runnable examples in examples/.

1. Create an HTML file

Load runtime/anima-runtime.js after the mount element. The path is relative to the folder containing your HTML file.

index.html · minimal host
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Hello Anima</title>
  <style>
    html, body, #app { margin:0; min-height:100%; }
    body { background:#070912; color:#f2f5ff; }
    #app { position:relative; min-height:100vh; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <div id="app"></div>
  <script src="../runtime/anima-runtime.js"></script>
  <script>
    const source = `
      app Hello {
        scene Home {
          node Screen {
            flow: column(cross: center, route: center, gap: 18);
            wide: "100%";
            tall: "100vh";
            fill: "#070912";
            ink: "#f2f5ff";
            node Title: Heading {
              text: "Hello, Anima.";
              scale: 56;
              weight: 300;
              motion: Reveal;
            }
            node Subtitle: Paragraph {
              text: "Structure, motion, and interaction in one source.";
              scale: 16;
              ink: "#9aa8c7";
              motion: FadeUp;
            }
          }
        }
      }
    `;
    const program = Anima.parse(source);
    Anima.mount(program, document.getElementById("app"));
  </script>
</body>
</html>
Copy this host template, then change the source between the backticks.

2. Write the program, then mount it

The Anima source is not JavaScript. It is text parsed by the runtime. Anima.parse(source) returns a program representation; Anima.mount(program, element) builds the first scene and binds event handlers.

Anima.parse(source)

Tokenizes and parses the custom language. Parse errors include a line and column for expected tokens.

Anima.mount(program, element)

Finds the app declaration, initializes state, renders the first scene, and returns an object containing state and app.

02 / Program model

Four structural building blocks.

Anima programs are organized around an app, state declarations, scenes, and nested nodes. Properties and event clauses live inside nodes.

app

The outer program block. The runtime expects an app declaration and mounts the last app declaration it finds.

state

Defines a named initial value: number, string, color, boolean, array, or object. Current state support is initialization and expression lookup, not a reactive state system.

scene

A screen/page. The first scene is mounted initially. Use go("SceneName") to navigate.

node

A named UI element nested inside another node or a scene. A node name becomes an anima-* CSS class.

Program shape
app MyApp {
  state title = "Welcome";
  state accent = "#75ddff";

  scene Home {
    node Screen {
      flow: column(cross: center, route: center);
      text: title;
      ink: accent;
    }
  }
}
Declarations can be separated by whitespace and optional semicolons after state values.
03 / Language reference

Syntax & expressions.

The lexer recognizes identifiers, quoted strings, numeric values with optional unit suffixes, hex colors, booleans, null, arrays, objects, operators, and function calls.

Comments and values

Value examples
// A single-line comment
/* A multi-line
   comment */

state count = 3;
state title = "Hello, world!";
state accent = #75ddff;
state visible = true;
state optional = null;
state steps = [1, 2, 3];
state theme = { ink: "#ffffff", fill: "#070912" };

String and object values are safest when quoted consistently. Bare identifiers evaluate as a state value when a matching state exists; otherwise they evaluate to their own name, which is how tokens such as center, column, and motion names are represented.

Operators

CategoryOperatorsPurpose
Logical|| &&Boolean-style OR and AND.
Comparison== != < > <= >=Equality is strict internally; relational comparisons use JavaScript comparison behavior.
Arithmetic+ - * / %Numeric operations; + also concatenates when one side is a string.
Unary! -Logical NOT and numeric negation.
Member / call. :: ()Read object properties and call functions exposed by the runtime.

Expression example

Read state values in a property
app Expressions {
  state product = "Anima";
  state edition = 1;
  state label = "Version " + edition;

  scene Home {
    node Screen {
      flow: column(cross: center, route: center, gap: 12);
      tall: "100vh";
      node Title: Heading { text: product; }
      node Version: Small { text: label; }
    }
  }
}
Expressions are evaluated when the node is rendered; this does not create reactive bindings.
!
Important: there is no general-purpose function declaration syntax, assignment operator, loop construct, array indexing syntax, or reactive update primitive in the current runtime. Avoid treating Anima as a JavaScript replacement or assuming all conventional programming features exist.
04 / Property reference

One vocabulary for the surface.

These are the property names understood by the current runtime. Values are evaluated, then translated to DOM content, classes, inline styles, or layout behavior. CSS values are usually provided as strings; numeric values are converted to pixels except for a small set of unitless CSS properties.

Content & type

text

Sets the node's text content.

class

Adds one or more classes separated by spaces.

mask

Sets a CSS mask image and centers it with contain sizing.

Color & appearance

fill

Background color, gradient, or image.

ink

Text color.

gradient

Applies a background gradient clipped to the text.

edge

Border string.

halo

Box-shadow string.

veil

Opacity, normally between 0 and 1.

backdrop

Backdrop filter, such as blur and saturation.

curve

Border radius.

filter

CSS filter string.

Typography

scale

Font size. Numeric values become px.

weight

Font weight, commonly 100–900.

voice

Font-family string.

style

Font-style string.

tracking

Letter spacing; a number becomes em.

leading

Line height.

anchor

Text alignment: start, center, end, just.

case

Text transform: upper, lower, capital, normal.

Size, spacing & positioning

wide

Width.

tall

Height.

cap

Maximum width.

minTall

Minimum height.

maxTall

Maximum height.

aspect

Aspect ratio.

inset

Padding.

offset

Margin.

gap

CSS gap, usually for flex layouts.

place

Position: free, anchor, stick, lock, float.

top / left / right / bottom

Offset edges for positioned nodes.

layer

z-index.

clip

Overflow behavior.

flex

Flex shorthand value.

order

Flex order.

alignSelf

CSS align-self.

transform

CSS transform string.

pointerEvents

CSS pointer-events value.

Background images

bgImage

background-image.

bgSize

background-size.

bgPos

background-position.

bgRepeat

background-repeat.

↳
Numeric values: scale: 28 becomes a 28px font size. A property mapped to CSS normally also receives px for a numeric value unless the target CSS property is unitless. Use quoted strings for values like "100%", "100vh", gradients, rgba colors, multi-value padding, and shadows.
05 / Layout

Flow first. Fine control when needed.

The flow property is interpreted by the runtime rather than mapped directly to a CSS property. It configures a small flex-layout vocabulary.

FormBehaviorOptions
columnFlex container, children flow vertically.gap, cross, route, wrap
rowFlex container, children flow horizontally.Same options.
trailHorizontal flow alias—useful for a row of controls.Same options.
hiddenSets display to none.No layout options applied.
freeSets display to block.No flex options applied.

Cross-axis alignment

cross accepts start, center, end, or stretch. It maps to flex item alignment.

Main-axis alignment

route accepts start, center, end, spread/space-between, or even/space-evenly.

Example

Centered row
node Actions {
  flow: trail(gap: 12, cross: center, wrap: true);
  node Primary: Button {
    text: "Continue";
  }
  node Secondary: Button {
    text: "Cancel";
  }
}

Liquid-glass surface

A practical example of the native vocabulary mapped to familiar CSS effects.

Frosted panel
node GlassPanel {
  flow: column(gap: 10);
  inset: "22px 26px";
  curve: 22;
  fill: "rgba(255,255,255,0.055)";
  backdrop: "blur(18px) saturate(180%)";
  edge: "1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.17)";
  halo: "0 18px 60px rgba(0,0,0,0.35)";
  node Title: Heading {
    text: "Liquid glass";
    scale: 24;
    weight: 550;
  }
}
The backdrop effect depends on browser support and the content behind the panel.
06 / Motion system

Animation as a property.

The runtime calls the Web Animations API for built-in motion names. A motion can be applied on mount with motion: or played in response to a signal.

MotionRuntime behaviorTypical use
RevealOpacity, upward movement, and blur resolve into view.Hero titles and important content.
FadeInOpacity transitions from 0 to 1.Subtle entrance.
FadeUpFade plus a short upward movement.Supporting copy and cards.
GlowSlow repeating opacity/scale breathing effect.Ambient background elements.
PulseScale up and back to its resting size.Press feedback or emphasis.

Compose motion

Motion grammar has four operators: pipe for sequence, ampersand for parallel play, star for repetition, and tilde for reversal. A star is followed by a count.

Motion expressions
// Reveal, then pulse twice
motion: Reveal | Pulse * 2;

// Play both motions together
motion: FadeIn & Pulse;

// Reverse a single named motion
motion: ~Reveal;

// Delay a motion by 400 milliseconds
motion: Reveal.delay(400);

// Repeat a motion through a modifier
motion: Pulse.repeat(3);
!
Implementation detail: the current executor fully handles simple named motions, sequence, parallel composition, repetition, reversal for simple keyframe motions, and .delay(ms)/.repeat(n). The parser also recognizes a .stagger(ms) modifier, but the current playback executor has no stagger handler, so do not depend on it yet. Complex reverse/composition combinations should be tested before production use.

Attach motion to a node

Entrance and interaction
node CallToAction: Button {
  text: "Explore Anima";
  fill: "#75ddff";
  ink: "#07111c";
  inset: "14px 22px";
  curve: 999;
  motion: FadeUp;
  on press: Pulse;
}

The runtime detects prefers-reduced-motion: reduce. When it is enabled, entrance motions are reduced to a brief opacity change and scene transitions skip the fade overlay.

07 / Signals & sound

Give nodes a response.

A node can listen to one or more signals. A signal clause either resolves a motion name or calls a function exposed in the runtime environment.

SignalBrowser eventNotes
presspointerdownStarts as soon as a pointer is pressed, not on release.
clickclickUsually best for actions that should activate on click/tap.
hoverpointerenterRuns when the pointer enters the node.
focusfocusRuns when the node receives focus.
Other event namesUsed directlyThe current runtime passes unrecognized signal names directly to addEventListener.

Runtime functions

go("SceneName")

Switches to the named scene if it exists and is not already the active scene. Unknown scene names are ignored.

chime(880)

Creates a short layered sine-wave chime at the supplied base frequency in hertz. If omitted, the base frequency is 880 Hz.

An interactive node
node SoundButton: Button {
  text: "Play a chime";
  inset: "14px 20px";
  curve: 999;
  fill: "rgba(117,221,255,0.12)";
  edge: "1px solid rgba(117,221,255,0.4)";
  on click: chime(660);
  on press: Pulse;
  on hover: FadeUp;
}
Browser audio may require a user gesture; the example uses a click signal to initialize audio.
08 / Scenes

Multi-screen without a router.

Scenes are named blocks inside the app. The first scene declared is the initial screen. Call the built-in go function from a signal handler to change the active scene. In the standard runtime, navigation crossfades through a dark veil unless reduced motion is requested.

Runnable · two scenes
app TwoScenes {
  scene Home {
    node Screen {
      flow: column(cross: center, route: center, gap: 18);
      wide: "100%";
      tall: "100vh";
      fill: "#070912";
      ink: "#f5f7ff";
      node Title: Heading {
        text: "Home";
        scale: 48;
        weight: 300;
        motion: Reveal;
      }
      node Next: Button {
        text: "Open details";
        inset: "13px 20px";
        curve: 999;
        fill: "#75ddff";
        ink: "#061019";
        on click: go("Details");
      }
    }
  }
  scene Details {
    node Screen {
      flow: column(cross: center, route: center, gap: 18);
      wide: "100%";
      tall: "100vh";
      fill: "#0d0b1d";
      ink: "#f5f7ff";
      node Title: Heading {
        text: "Details";
        scale: 48;
        weight: 300;
        motion: Reveal;
      }
      node Back: Button {
        text: "Back home";
        inset: "13px 20px";
        curve: 999;
        fill: "rgba(171,136,255,0.18)";
        ink: "#f5f7ff";
        on click: go("Home");
      }
    }
  }
}
Run the preview to test navigation. Preview is isolated in an iframe.

Node names and external CSS

Every node name becomes a normalized class prefixed with anima-. For example, node HeroCard produces a class like anima-hero-card. The runtime still generates inline styles for Anima properties; external CSS can supplement these defaults and target named nodes.

HTML-side CSS supplement
/* Include this in the host HTML stylesheet */
.anima-hero-card {
  transition: transform 220ms ease, border-color 220ms ease;
}
.anima-hero-card:hover {
  transform: translateY(-3px);
}
10 / Runtime API

Three public entry points.

APIArgumentsBehavior
Anima.lex(source)Source stringReturns the token stream. Useful for inspecting how the lexer reads source.
Anima.parse(source)Source stringReturns a program AST with a decls array containing parsed app declarations.
Anima.mount(program, container)Parsed program; DOM elementInitializes app state, mounts the first scene, attaches signal handlers, and returns { state, app }.

Full host bootstrap

The minimum runtime call
const program = Anima.parse(source);
const mounted = Anima.mount(program, document.getElementById("app"));

// Runtime return value:
console.log(mounted.state);
console.log(mounted.app);

The current runtime exposes go and chime in the expression environment for use in signal handlers. There is no supported external reactive setter or general user-defined function registration API in this source version.

11 / Troubleshooting

Common gotchas.

The page stays blank

Check that the runtime script loads before calling Anima.parse, that the program contains an app block with at least one scene, and that the mount element exists. Inspect the browser console for parser or DOM errors.

A click does not work

Verify the node has on click: go("Target") or another supported function call. The target scene name must match exactly. Use click for activation on release; press fires at pointer down.

A style is ignored

Only properties in this guide are mapped. Property names that look like CSS but are not in the mapping are generally ignored. Prefer Anima names such as fill, ink, curve, inset, and halo. Use quoted strings for CSS values containing punctuation.

A motion does not play

Use one of the five implemented motion names: Reveal, FadeIn, FadeUp, Glow, or Pulse. Check reduced-motion preferences if an effect appears simplified.

Audio is silent

Browsers often block audio until a user gesture. Trigger chime() from a click handler and check device volume. Audio support is implemented through the Web Audio API.

My state change does not update the screen

That is a current runtime limitation. State values initialize and can be read in expressions, but the current runtime doesn't have assignment or reactive re-render support for app state.

12 / Runtime status

What works today—and what doesn't.

This section intentionally separates executable features from claims or examples in the older landing-page copy. The implementation is a compact runtime; it is not yet a full general-purpose web framework or a complete reactive language.

CapabilityStatus in current sourceNotes
App / scene / node parsingImplementedCustom lexer and recursive parser are included in the runtime.
Mapped styles and flex flowImplementedSee complete mapping and flow options above.
Five named motionsImplementedReveal, FadeIn, FadeUp, Glow, Pulse.
Motion compositionPartialSequence, parallel, repeat, reverse, delay are handled; modifier behavior has limits.
Click/press/hover/focus handlersImplementedOther event names are passed directly to the DOM listener.
Scene navigationImplementedgo("SceneName") with a dark veil transition.
Generated chimeImplementedchime(freq) uses Web Audio oscillators.
Reactive state mutationNot implementedState initializes and reads, but there is no setter/assignment or reactive redraw API.
Timeline declarationsNot implementedThe original page mentions timeline Score; the parser does not parse timeline blocks in this runtime.
Additional names like Bloom / Ripple / Line / TwinkleNot implementedThey appear in older copy, but are not in the runtime's motion registry.
Loops / array iterationNot implementedArrays and objects parse as values; there is no loop syntax.
Native compilation / package ecosystemRoadmap ideaNot part of the included browser runtime.
!
Parser caution: in some contexts the parser advances past unknown tokens instead of raising a descriptive error. A typo may therefore result in missing behavior. Keep examples close to the documented grammar and validate the result in a browser while developing.
13 / Roadmap notes

The original direction, preserved.

The earlier Anima site outlined a longer-term direction. These are archived product ideas from that source—not a commitment, schedule, or claim that they work in the current runtime.

Proposed · 1.1

Native compilation

Explore a C# compiler front-end and native output targets, reusing a compatible subset of Anima source.

Proposed · 2.0

Language ecosystem

Explore package and component sharing, an editor, autocomplete, design-system namespaces, and visual motion inspection.

The product principles in the original site remain useful as design goals: one vocabulary for structure and motion, readable native terms, browser portability, motion-aware design, and respect for reduced-motion preferences.
